name: Marco Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What is an ordinary shift like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 58 and a junior operator on a spice-sachet sealing line. I finished secondary school and only moved from warehouse picking into the machine room this year. I feed film rolls, watch the heat seal and check the first sachets for leaks. I still ask the lead operator before changing a setting.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How are things at home, and do you use AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner manages a school kitchen; our grown children live away from home. My late shift pays above the normal operator rate, and we have roughly a year's expenses saved. There are plenty of other packing plants nearby. I use AI now and then for a recipe or a travel route, once someone I trust has tried the tool. I'd like to stop at 66 in 2034 if documented income after work can actually cover our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the packing crew that a dull forecast does not make a broken seal harmless. We still need someone to open the first sachet, and the lead operator needs paid time to teach new starters. I would raise that at the union meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The late-shift rate and our savings give us room to breathe. I am still learning the sealer, so I don't confuse a high wage with being the best operator in the room. If the line stays much the same, I can build experience and check whether 66 is truly affordable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep pulling the first ten sachets after each film change and record any leak with the lead operator. I'll take that record to the union safety meeting so guards and paid training stay on the rota. My partner and I will continue adding fresh pay to our reserve after bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about our household money for now. A junior sealer can learn a lot from ten opened spice sachets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the first leaking sachet show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A pinhole leaves spice dust around the sealed edge. I stop the feed and ask the lead operator to test the heat bar before the next carton. I do not change a hot setting on a hunch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why can the household save now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The late rate is higher than the usual operator pay, and my partner has regular kitchen hours. That is why we have about a year saved. I still want an income calculation before I call 2034 our retirement year.

say: **First-sachet checks** remain useful even if AI mostly fades.
The union should protect **paid teaching** and guarded sealer work.
think: Our **higher shift pay** and year of savings make current bills manageable.
I am still **junior at sealing** and need experience before planning an exit.
do: **Check** the first ten sachets after film changes with the lead.
**Bring** leak records to the union and add new wages to the reserve after bills.
feel: **Calm** about current income while learning the familiar line.
S0.quote: A junior sealer can learn a lot from ten opened spice sachets.
fieldNote: His **higher late-shift pay**, regular partner income and year saved support a calm baseline despite junior skill.
The **union safety meeting** is real group activity; reserve additions come from current pay, not funds already held.

steps.text: Check first ten sachets with lead after film changes
Bring leak record to union safety meeting
Save new late-shift wages after household bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say software may plan spice orders and labels before robots handle hot film. I would use a tested screen if it helps us catch the wrong batch, but I want the lead beside me for any machine change. The union should make the practice paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Planning changes could mean shorter runs and fewer late shifts. Our reserve would cushion that, but I would not want to lose the premium just as we are trying to settle the retirement numbers. I can learn a proven display; I cannot learn a hot sealer safely from a chat box.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask the lead to show me the plant's batch-check screen after another operator has tested it, if management permits me to use it on paid time. I'll compare the posted late rota and premium with recent pay slips, then bring a real shortfall to our union rep. If a paid guarded seal-check course is offered, I'll enrol and practise on a stopped line with the lead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a possible cut to my own premium, but there is room to check and respond. A tidy order screen will not put a missing evening shift back on my pay slip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you learn on the batch-check screen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd match the batch number, spice name and film code on the screen to the paper job card. If they differ, I would stop and ask the lead before starting a run. That is a new display skill; my occasional recipe searches do not cover it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you prove a premium cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the posted late shifts and premium line with four actual pay slips. If the hours or rate fall, the rep gets the numbers, not a rumour. A full reserve does not make a pay cut pleasant.

say: **Order software** may change batches before robots handle hot film.
A tested display needs **paid supervised practice** for junior operators.
think: Shorter runs could reduce my **late premium** before retirement is funded.
I can learn a **proven screen**, but a hot machine still needs a lead operator.
do: **Learn** the permitted batch screen on paid time after another operator tests it.
**Compare** rota and pay, raise real cuts with the union, and attend offered paid guarded seal practice.
feel: **Anxious** about a possible premium cut despite the strong reserve.
S1.quote: A tidy order screen will not put a missing evening shift back on my pay slip.
fieldNote: His **occasional home AI use** is separate from learning the plant batch screen with permission and paid supervision.
The **seal course** requires an offered paid guarded place; the union claim uses actual posted shifts and payslips.

steps.text: Learn permitted tested batch screen with lead on paid shift
Compare posted late rota and premium with four pay slips
Bring documented late-premium cut to union rep
Enrol in seal-check course if paid guarded place offered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that thinking AI could run orders by 2028, and robots able to pack sachets might arrive around 2031 when I am 63. I want written staffing dates before a supplier's demonstration becomes our new rota. The union can ask for that together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the line to lose many late shifts if robots can seal and box sachets. A year's savings and nearby plants give us options, but neither proves we can stop at 63. I'd need another wage until the figures show we can afford retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask the union rep to seek written shift plans and funded paid guarded seal-inspection places. If a place is actually offered, I'll enrol and pass the practical leak test. If my hours fall, I'll apply to posted safe local packing jobs only when net pay after travel covers our bills; after qualifying, I'll also apply to posted inspection jobs on those terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, because a large wage cut is possible, but the reserve gives us time to find another line. I can act on a posting; I cannot act on a supplier's promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would seal-inspection training involve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would need to identify a weak heat seam, stop the guarded machine and reject the faulty carton. A lead should watch me do that on paid time. I would not spend our household reserve on a company-required course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes a nearby job viable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The job must be actually posted, with its base wage, paid hours and site. I would take off travel and compare what remains with our bills. For inspection, I would need the practical qualification before applying.

say: **2031 robots** might take sachet shifts while I am 63.
The union should obtain **written staffing dates** and funded practical places.
think: Many **late shifts** could be lost before retirement is affordable.
A **year saved** and plentiful local plants offer choices, not guaranteed income.
do: **Seek** written shift plans and funded paid guarded inspection through the union.
**Apply** to real safe local packing or qualified inspection jobs if hours fall and net pay covers bills.
feel: **Anxious** about a possible large pay loss, with savings and local options.
S2.quote: I can act on a posting; I cannot act on a supplier's promise.
fieldNote: He expects **many late shifts** to go but retains a year of savings and several nearby packing plants.
The **inspection path** needs funded paid guarded training, qualification and a posted safe local role at sufficient net pay.

steps.text: Ask union for written shifts and funded paid guarded inspection
Enrol in seal inspection if funded paid guarded place offered
Apply to posted safe local packing if hours fall and net pay covers bills
Apply to posted safe local inspection if qualified, hours fall, net pay covers bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI might plan spice orders by 2031 and capable robots reach the sealer around 2034, when I am 66. That is the age I hope to stop. I would rather check the household figures now than tell everyone I am already out of danger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If documented income after work covers our bills at 66, robot sealing may arrive after I have left. If it does not, I may need the late premium for longer. The strong reserve helps with a move, but I would still need a decent paid role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner and I will list bills and get written figures for income available after I stop. I'll keep adding fresh late-shift pay to savings while we check. If I am still employed in 2034 and shifts fall, I'll apply to posted safe local packing only if net pay after travel covers our costs; I'll enrol in funded paid guarded seal inspection if an offered place is required for a posted inspection job, then apply after qualifying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious until the numbers are checked, because the sealer could change in the very year I hope to stop. My 66th birthday will not replace a sealer pay slip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which retirement figures would you check?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We need monthly income after my wage ends, set beside rent, food and the travel my partner pays. I cannot assume a payment from an unverified scheme. If the gap is there, I keep working and look at a real posted role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes for an inspection posting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A packing role would need a safe paid shift and enough net wage after travel. An inspection posting adds a passed practical check from an offered funded paid guarded place. I would not leave the higher-paid line for a headline wage that does not reach the kitchen table.

say: **2031 order AI** comes before sealer robots around my hoped-for stop at 66.
A retirement date needs **documented household income**.
think: If the figures fail, I may still need the **late-shift premium** in 2034.
Our **year of savings** helps a job move, not indefinite living without wages.
do: **Check** actual post-work income and keep saving new late-shift wages.
**Apply** to safe posted local packing if still employed and hours fall; train and qualify for posted inspection.
feel: **Anxious** until verified income shows whether stopping at 66 is affordable.
S3.quote: My 66th birthday will not replace a sealer pay slip.
fieldNote: His **2034 stop** is conditional on documented income; robot arrival in that year makes the timing consequential.
A **later inspection application** requires continued work, lost shifts, offered funded paid guarded training, qualification and viable net pay.

steps.text: Compare documented post-work income with monthly household bills
Enrol in inspection if funded paid guarded place offered for posted job
Apply to posted safe local packing if employed in 2034, hours fall, net pay sufficient
Apply to posted safe local inspection if qualified, employed in 2034, hours fall, net pay sufficient

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI could plan our orders in 2036 when I am 68 and robots might handle sachets around 2039 when I am 71. If our retirement sums work, I will have left the late shift in 2034. If not, I still want a real wage and a safe machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We have about a year of expenses saved, not a lifetime. I hope to stop at 66, but I need actual income after work to pay the bills. A ten-year warning lets us check rather than pretend savings alone will do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year my partner and I will put documented income after work beside rent, food and other costs. I'll keep the paid sealer shift and add new wages to savings while we decide. If the figures make 2034 affordable, I'll stop then; if I am still working after 2036 and hours fall, I'll apply to posted safe local packing jobs only when the net wage after travel covers our costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy until the income is verified, but ten years gives us breathing space. Our savings can buy time to decide; they cannot pay every future bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes the 2034 stop affordable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We need the actual monthly income that would arrive when my wage stops. We will subtract our ordinary bills and leave room for a surprise repair. A year saved does not mean a pension cheque exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you send a later application?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would look for a real posting with safe guards, paid hours and a base wage that works after travel. I would only apply if I were still working and my shifts had fallen after 2036. If I have retired affordably, there is no application to send.

say: **2036 AI** and later robots allow time to check household income.
I hope for a **2034 exit** only if post-work money covers bills.
think: A **year saved** cannot replace regular income for life.
If retirement fails the sums, I may still be **working after 2036**.
do: **Compare** documented post-work income with bills and keep earning and saving meanwhile.
**Apply** only if still employed after 2036, hours fall and a posted safe local job pays enough net.
Stop **work in 2034** only if documented post-work income covers rent and ordinary household costs.
feel: **Uneasy** about unverified retirement income, with time and savings for decisions.
S4.quote: A year saved does not mean a pension cheque exists.
fieldNote: The **retirement comparison** is a request for facts; no future benefit or confirmed exit is assumed.
Any **post-2036 job search** requires continued employment, lost hours and an actual safe local posting with adequate net pay.

steps.text: Compare documented post-work income with monthly household bills
Keep paid sealer shifts until affordable planned retirement in 2034; otherwise continue while paid
Save new late-shift wages after bills
Apply to posted safe local packing if employed after 2036, hours fall, net pay sufficient

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast 2028 case. Losing a lot of the late shift at 63 would unsettle our plan before we know whether stopping at 66 is affordable. Written staffing dates, a funded paid guarded inspection place and actual safe local postings with adequate net pay would help. The year saved gives us time, not a replacement wage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what happens to the first spice sachet after a film roll changes. One pinhole can perfume a whole carton before the line shows a fault.

headlineQuote: One pinhole can perfume a whole carton before the line shows a fault.
portrait: **Marco**, 58, is a junior spice-sachet sealer operator with secondary schooling and occasional checked AI use.
He and his school-kitchen-manager partner have **grown children**, higher late-shift pay, a year saved and many nearby packing plants.
His **progressive outlook** brings safety and paid training to the union, while his steady adaptability waits for a tool others have tested.
He is **anxious** about possible fast shift loss; stopping at 66 depends on documented post-work income covering bills.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** may bring sealer robots around 2031 and cut late shifts at age 63 before retirement is affordable.
whatWouldHelp: **Written staffing dates**, funded paid guarded inspection and real safe local postings with adequate net pay would help.
